attribution.note: Marcus's own concluding sentence in his post, in his own voice.

semantics.note: A causal claim that scaling made AI enshittification worse rather than better. The normalisation keeps both the 'not better' and the 'worse' parts.

contract.note: Reading scaling as model size, data or compute is the ordinary technical reading of his 'magic sauce' phrase. Requiring evidence that separates scaling from other changes is demanding, but a causal claim needs it. Enshittification has no stated measure, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: Scaled-up, shaped-up models give confident wrong answers more often. This bundles scaling with shaping and does not measure public content harm.
Newer models overgeneralise science summaries more. Model vintage is not a controlled scaling change, and no downstream harm is measured.
GPT-4 fabricated far fewer citations than GPT-3.5. This cuts against uniform worsening but does not isolate scaling or its net effect.

reviews.rationale: No item isolates the effect of scaling on the production or spread of low-quality content. The packet points both ways: e1 and e2 show some reliability getting worse, while e3 shows fewer citation errors. All three confound scaling with other changes, so the causal claim stays unsettled on this packet.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. He cites Science, but the assertion that things got 'much worse' is his.

semantics.note: 'That' refers to GenAI enshittifying science, as discussed in his March 2024 post. Treating the period as March 2024 onward and the claim as an observation is faithful.

contract.note: Reading 'much worse' as a substantial rise in unreliable AI-caused scientific material is the ordinary reading. No threshold is given, so the magnitude test is the evaluator's choice.

evidence.note: An arXiv-wide citation audit shows hallucinated references accelerating in early 2025. It supports the direction of change, but the method is narrow, false positives are acknowledged, and the absolute rate is low.
Organised fraud is growing, but the study does not measure AI's share of that growth.

reviews.rationale: e1 supports a worsening trend in one narrow metric (hallucinated arXiv citations) before the post. Nothing in the packet establishes the broad, substantial increase that 'much worse' needs under the contract. The Science-linked study is about fraud and does not isolate AI. The direction is supported but the magnitude is unsettled.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: A general causal claim about AI-assisted science. 'Will' is firm wording, not hedged. The 'significant fraction' threshold and the hallucination cause are both kept.

contract.note: Reading the claim as a nontrivial share of AI-assisted scientific work containing material falsehoods caused by hallucination is a fair, ordinary reading of 'significant fraction... wrong'.

evidence.note: Shows hallucinated citations at scale after LLM adoption, published before the cutoff. It gives no paper-level share of materially wrong AI-assisted work, and its attribution is statistical.
A purpose-built LLM agent wrote accurate scientific summaries. This limits any 'inevitable failure' inference but gives no population rate.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows widespread hallucinated citations but has no denominator of AI-assisted work and no measured fraction of materially wrong findings. Citation defects are not the same as wrong science. The counterevidence shows only that some well-designed workflows are accurate. The packet does not settle the claim either way.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. The Nick Cave quote is an aside and is not scored.

semantics.note: 'Everywhere' is hyperbole, but the named sectors make the breadth testable. The normalisation lists them faithfully.

contract.note: Reading 'everywhere' as documented problematic AI content in each named sector, not high prevalence, is the ordinary reading of this rhetoric. Using 2025 up to the post date as the window is reasonable.

evidence.note: Journalism: the publisher admits its supplement printed an AI-generated list of nonexistent books (May 2025).
Law: a June 2025 High Court judgment records fictitious citations and an admission that AI tools were used.
Music: Deezer's own platform disclosure reports many AI uploads and fraudulent streams. The 0.5% listening share limits prevalence, not presence.
Politics/government: an FBI notice describes AI voice impersonation of senior US officials from April 2025.
Education: secondary reporting of defective AI-made course materials, with the professor's admission (Feb 2025).

reviews.rationale: Dated records from the 2025 window document problematic AI-generated content in all five named sectors, which meets the contract's breadth test. The Deezer item is a company disclosure, and the education example rests on secondary reporting. Deezer's 0.5% listening share limits how prevalent AI music is, but the claim as read is about presence, not prevalence.
